content.text: Around 1.8 million people die from diarrhoeal diseases globally, 90 per cent of whom are children under five, mostly in developing countries. In Pakistan, 630 children die each day from water-borne illnesses. Experts at the first day of Aga Khan University's National Health Sciences Research Symposium on the Impact of Water and Sanitation on Health: Our Problems, Our Solutions, pointed out that clean drinking water and sanitation problems are known and what Pakistan needs is to implement the solutions available through partnerships between government and civil society.

Pakistan has been unable to meet the drinking water demand of a rapidly growing population. Ninety per cent of water is used for agriculture and less than 10 per cent for drinking and sanitation. This means, said Dr Iqtidar A Khan, Chair, Organising Committee of the Symposium, that water availability has fallen from 5,000 cubic metres per capita in the early 1950s to less than 1,500 cubic metres today. The country is on the way to becoming water-scarce - when water availability falls below 1,000 cubic metres per capita annually. Dr Khan quoted the words of Kofi Annan, former Secretary-General of the United Nations, that AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria and other infectious diseases will not be defeated until the battle for safe drinking water, sanitation and basic health care are won.

Water and sanitation are a cornerstone for economic development and all people, including the poor, should have right of access todrinking water and sanitation services,said UNICEF Deputy Representative, Luc Chauvin. Water, sanitation and poverty are linked: diseases brought on by poor quality drinking water and inadequate sanitation facilities mean that people lose income opportunities and incur increased health costs. Improving access to water and sanitation will help reduce Pakistan's health burden.

Environmental design has played a vital role in linking water and health, from Mohenjo Daro to metropolitan Boston. Dr James Wescoat, Professor at Aga Khan Program for Islamic Architecture at MIT pointed out that in particular, landscape planning has a growing role to play in helping "scale-up" household and neighbourhood water and sanitation solutions to rural and urban landscapes; and, also, to help "scale-down" the potential water and health effects of global environmental change to solutions for communities. Drawing on a well-known study, he described how landscape planning and design - from site layout to grading, drainage, water harvesting, and ecological planting - can help reduce the spread of diseases and limit their risks.

Senior Architect and Urban Town Planner, Arif Hassan underlined the fact that over thelast 50 years the government has invested considerable money, including aid, in drinking water and sanitation programmes. However, these projects have not been successful and have increased Pakistan's foreign debt considerably. Some NGO projects have delivered but unless their methodology becomes a part of official policy, and planning and implementation procedures, they cannot achieve the scale that is required for servicing the growing demand for water and sanitation. In the past two years, the government has legislated a sanitation and drinking water policy which, to be successful, will need to relate to realities on the ground.

Low-cost sanitation technology is available. Addressing the Symposium via the internet, Dr Bindeshwar Pathak, founder of the Sulabh Sanitary Movement, India, shared his experience of introducing a two-pit pour flush toilet that uses only 1-1.5 litres of water. The resulting sludge can be safely cleaned and converted into rich organic manure. The technology is flexible and affordable and can be implemented at costs ranging from US$ 30 (Rs 2,400) upwards
Dr Rashid Jooma, Director General Health, Government of Pakistan, and the chief guest, pointed out that the estimated cost of environmental degradation in Pakistan is 365.
